current_example.problem:
Complete the truth table below and use it to determine whether $(A \land B) \Rightarrow (B \Rightarrow A)$ is a tautology.

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\, A \land B \,$ | $\, B \Rightarrow A \,$ | $\, (A\land B) \Rightarrow (B \Rightarrow A) \,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |  |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |  |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ |  |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |  |
current_example.worked_solution:
An expression is a tautology if it is always true, regardless of the inputs.

By completing the final column in the truth table below, we obtain the following:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\, A \land B \,$ | $\, B \Rightarrow A \,$ | $\, (A\land B) \Rightarrow (B \Rightarrow A) \,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ |

According to the table, $(A \land B) \Rightarrow (B \Rightarrow A)$ is always true. Therefore, it is a tautology.
